how.lead: No source gives a damage percentage for a flame-length class. So the six values were set in three moves: evidence fixes the direction and the ordering, written rules say what each class means, and a judged number is put on each meaning. The table was then checked against published evidence, without being fitted to it.

steps.d: The US Forest Service fire simulation (FSim) orders its six classes by flame length. It supports the order. It does not say how much heat reaches a panel, or for how long.
refs: USDA Forest Service, FSim wildfire risk components, RDS-2016-0034-3 (2023)

steps.t: A panel can be damaged by fire heat, and may need replacing
steps.d: Lab tests show panel glass cracking and burning through under heat (Wang 2025 reports tolerance mostly in the range of 8 to 15 kW/m² of radiant heat; Zhao 2026 shows tilt and glass condition change the result). A field study of a wildfire-affected plant found hot spots and degradation. These show the mechanism. None says how many panels are lost in a given class.
refs: Wang, Xiao and Bedon (2025), PV panels under thermal loading
Zhao et al. (2026), single-glass PV modules in pool fire
Jang et al. (2026), PV modules after wildfire, field diagnostics

steps.t: Why the lab numbers cannot set the values
steps.d: The lab results are in heat at the panel. The fire data is in flame-length classes. Field measurements show the heat from a wildland fire varies widely with fuel, distance and geometry, so there is no defensible conversion from a class to heat at a panel. Without it, a lab threshold cannot be placed on the class scale.
refs: Frankman et al. (2012), convective and radiative heating in wildland fires
Butler (2010), convective heating in full-scale crown fires

steps.t: So rules say what each class means, and a number is judged for it
steps.d: The cell writes down what each class stands for, from “near zero” to “major loss, but not automatic total loss”, keeps every value below 0.90, and keeps the table rising. The number put on each meaning is engineering judgement.

cols: What the class is taken to mean
rows: Near zero, but not zero for exposed plastics and electronics
No meaning of its own: set between its neighbours, rising
First detectable damage across several parts, without broad replacement
Substantial replacement of exposed and electronic parts
Major loss across subsystems, but not automatic total loss
checks: Forest Service field measurements show severe fires can deliver large, short bursts of heat, so heavy damage in the top classes is physically possible.
PV fire tests show the outcome depends on the panel’s build, its glass, its tilt and the duration, which supports a gradual rise and not one sharp threshold.
DOE/FEMP guidance says burned sections are generally rebuilt, and heat-affected panels need infrared and electroluminescence inspection.
The cell also runs every value at 0.6 and 1.5 times: a stress test, not a confidence range.
checkRefs: DOE/FEMP, Solar PV Hardening for Resilience: Wildfire

rules: The lowest class stays near zero, a little above it for exposed plastics and electronics.
The 4 to 6 ft class is the first with detectable damage to several parts, without broad replacement.
The 6 to 8 ft class means material local replacement.
The 8 to 12 ft class allows substantial replacement of exposed and electronic parts.
The top class allows major loss across subsystems, but not automatic total loss.
Metal and buried parts stay below electronics and plastics.
